lessons.title: Types of Studies
lessons.intro: Distinguish study types and the scope and strength of their conclusions.

lessons.title: Random Sampling
lessons.intro: Recognize random sampling designs and explain their statistical benefits.

lessons.intro: Use blocks and matched pairs and distinguish causal inference from generalization.

questions.scenario: Researchers randomly select 200 residents and ask how many times they used a public park last month.
questions.prompt: Which of the following best classifies the investigation?
choices: A sample survey, because information is obtained by questioning selected residents.
An experiment, because park use is a treatment.
A census, because residents were selected randomly.
An observational study, because random selection defines observational studies.

steps: The researchers ask questions of a subset of residents.
They impose no treatment. A sample survey is the most specific correct description.
solution.warning: Random selection determines how units enter a study; it does not itself define the study type.

questions.scenario: A mechanic compares past maintenance records for buses that already use either steel or ceramic brake pads. The mechanic does not change the pads.
questions.prompt: Which of the following best classifies the investigation?
choices: A census, because every bus in the region was measured.
A retrospective observational study, because existing records provide the data.
An experiment, because the buses use different pad types.
A prospective study, because future records will be collected.

steps: The pad types were already in use, so no treatment was imposed.
The data come from past records, making the observational study retrospective.
solution.warning: Comparing existing groups does not turn an observational study into an experiment.

questions.scenario: An engineer randomly assigns 60 similar air filters to receive either coating A or coating B, then measures particles trapped.
questions.prompt: Which of the following best classifies the study?
choices: A sample survey, because 60 filters form a sample.
A census, because every manufactured filter is tested.
A randomized experiment, because the engineer assigns coatings at random.
An observational study, because particle counts are observed.

steps: The engineer actively assigns the explanatory condition, the coating.
Random assignment makes this a randomized experiment.
solution.warning: Every study observes outcomes; the defining feature of an experiment is the imposition of treatments.

questions.scenario: A housing association selects a random sample of its households to estimate average weekly water use.
questions.prompt: Which of the following is a benefit of selecting a random sample?
choices: It allows treatments to be randomly assigned.
It supports generalizing the estimate to the association's households.
It guarantees that the sample's water-use distribution matches the population exactly.
It establishes that household size causes water use.

steps: Random selection gives a probability-based link between the sampled households and the population.
It supports population inference while still allowing sampling variability.
solution.warning: Representativeness is not an exact-match guarantee, and random sampling alone does not establish causation.

questions.scenario: A city randomly samples 300 households and finds that households with a compost bin produce less mixed waste. No bins are assigned.
questions.prompt: Which of the following conclusions is justified?
choices: The results apply only to the 300 sampled households.
Random sampling removes every possible confounding variable.
Bin ownership is associated with mixed-waste production in the city's households.
Owning a bin causes every household to produce less mixed waste.

steps: Random sampling supports generalization to the city's households.
Because bin ownership was observed rather than randomly assigned, other household differences may explain the association.
solution.warning: Random sampling supports scope; random assignment supports a causal comparison.

questions.scenario: Forty volunteer ceramic artists are randomly assigned to use one of two glazes. A well-designed experiment finds a statistically significant difference in durability.
questions.prompt: Which of the following conclusions is best supported?
choices: The better glaze will improve durability for every artist.
No causal conclusion is possible because the artists volunteered.
The result automatically generalizes to all ceramic artists worldwide.
The glaze caused a durability difference for artists similar to these volunteers.

steps: Random assignment supports a causal comparison between the glazes.
Volunteer recruitment limits the population to artists similar to those who participated.
solution.warning: A randomized experiment can support causation without supporting unrestricted generalization.

questions.scenario: A school records the travel time of every student enrolled this term. No travel-time records are missing.
questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is correct?

questions.scenario: A grower wants to estimate mean fruit mass. Trees in each of three varieties produce similar masses, but the varieties have substantially different mean masses. The grower considers randomly sampling within each variety.
questions.prompt: Why is stratifying by variety useful?
choices: It can reduce variability in estimates of the overall mean fruit mass.
It automatically eliminates bias in the mass measurements.
It reduces variability in estimates of the proportion of trees belonging to each variety.
It guarantees that the sampled and population mean masses are identical.

steps: Variety explains substantial differences in fruit mass.
Sampling within every variety keeps random sample composition from varying unnecessarily across those groups.
solution.warning: Stratification targets variability of the response estimate, not automatic bias removal or exact agreement.

questions.scenario: A port authority wants strata that improve the precision of estimated average loading time.
questions.prompt: Which arrangement is most appropriate?
choices: A small number of very large groups regardless of loading-time differences
Groups with similar loading times within each group and different typical times between groups
Groups with loading times as different as possible within every group
Groups of equal size regardless of loading-time differences

steps: Useful strata group units alike on a characteristic related to the response.
Random selection within every such group can reduce variability of the overall estimate.
solution.warning: Equal-sized strata are not required, and internal heterogeneity weakens the precision benefit.

questions.scenario: A city proposes surveying every household on four randomly chosen streets. Streets differ greatly in housing type, which is related to the survey response.
questions.prompt: Which of the following is a statistical disadvantage of this cluster sample?

A cluster sample has no statistical disadvantages.

steps: Each street is a cluster, but the streets differ in a way related to the outcome.
Selecting only a few clusters can produce substantial variation in which housing types are represented.
